note: Per-population rights statements for The Zybach Collection. The material here was made at different times, under different agreements, by different people, for different institutions, so there is no single collection-level statement and no collection-level licence. Each group carries its own. Values are drawn from the RightsStatements.org vocabulary and are limited to InC, UND and InC-RUU. InC-EDU is never used: it asserts an authority to permit third-party educational use that the Library does not hold. No Creative Commons licence is applied to any source material, because a CC grant is irrevocable and the Library cannot give away rights that are not its own.

populations.label: The fifteen printed monographs
populations.gloss: Nobody's ownership of these printed volumes is documented, so the Library says so rather than guessing.
populations.detail: The volumes carry no copyright notice of any kind. That absence does not put them in the public domain — the rule that made a missing notice fatal reaches only works published before 1 March 1989, and every volume here is later. What the missing notice tells us is that ownership was never settled at the time. The title pages recite that the project was authorized and directed by the Director of the OSU Research Forests and funded by the OSU College of Forestry, but a funding recital is not an assignment.

populations.label: The creator's Letitia Carson writing
populations.gloss: His own articles, columns and research reports. He wrote them and he publishes them himself; the Library's copy is a display copy.
populations.detail: Four of these carry a text layer and are reproduced page by page: the 2014 ORWW research report written with Janet Meranda, two long articles in The Umpqua Trapper, and his entry in the online encyclopedia at BlackPast.org. Where an article appeared inside somebody else's periodical, only the pages of his own article are reproduced; the cover, masthead, notices and advertisements belong to the society that printed them and stay on his scan. The remainder of his writing is scanned without a text layer, and is catalogued and linked rather than reproduced. The Letitia Carson series contains four further populations besides this one — the public records, the Merandas' transcriptions, his photographs, and the third-party works in his reference library — each with its own statement below.

populations.label: The Letitia Carson public records
populations.statement: Public Domain in the United States
populations.gloss: Court, probate, homestead, land and citizenship records made by government officers in the nineteenth century. Nobody owns them.
populations.detail: Two hundred and fifty files in the creator's documentation folders: Ashe County citizenship papers, a Platte County deed, the Benton County probate of David Carson's estate, the two suits Letitia Carson brought against Greenberry Smith, and her homestead file. The Library describes each one, shows the creator's thumbnail where he made one, and links his full-size scan rather than making a second copy. The same statement covers the works in his reference library that were published before 1929 or made by a government — Palmer, Chittenden, Paxton, Lockley, Cummins, the Oregon Spectator indexes made by the W.P.A. in 1941, the Bureau of Land Management's homesteading history, and the General Land Office and USGS map sheets.

The Library states this in plain words rather than by a vocabulary code, because the vocabulary's no-copyright statements assert a jurisdiction determination the Library is not making for anyone else.
